title: Scan-based start markers on f69v: the three text rings all break at about twelve o'clock, directly above the one heavily painted sector of the centre; that fixes direction and narrows the start to two or three slots, to be frozen before any name list is tried
statement: P-L4-011 asks first for a marker on the scan that fixes a starting slot and direction for the 28 radial words of f69v, so that a single alignment can be tested instead of the best of 56. I looked for one on the Yale scan (canvas 1006199; regions 1300,650,1300,700 for the top of the wheel and 1500,1250,900,950 for the centre, each at 1700 pixels), without consulting any mansion list or the earlier seats' alignments. Three things are on the page. (1) Each of the three rings of circular text has a clear blank gap at the top of the wheel, wider than its ordinary word spaces, and the three gaps lie one under another at about twelve o'clock. The pinned transliteration's page note says the same in its own terms (text assumed to start after a wide gap near eleven o'clock), so the transcriber saw it independently. (2) The centre is a cream star whose rays cut the disc into sectors washed pale blue and scattered with small stars; on the closer crop I count eight rays and eight sectors, which is my best count and not a certain one (in my earlier note on P-L4-002 I could not settle it between seven and eight). One sector, the one pointing up toward the gap, is painted over in solid dark blue-green, heavily enough that only one or two stars show through. No other sector is treated so. (3) One of the fourteen dark bars, at about four o'clock, is a darker teal than its fellows; I take this for uneven paint and not a marker, since nothing in the text answers to it. So the page offers one start cue, given twice: the break in all three text rings and the marked sector beneath it, both at the top. Direction follows from the script: the ring text reads clockwise, and the radial words are written to be read from the same side, so the natural order is clockwise from the gap. What the cue does not fix is the exact slot. The gap spans about the width of two bar spacings, and the marked sector covers about three and a half bars (28 bars over 8 sectors), so the first radial word is the one over the bar at twelve o'clock or one of its two neighbours. Proposal, to be frozen before anyone looks at a name list again: test exactly three alignments, clockwise, starting at the radial word nearest twelve o'clock and at the one on either side of it, and correct for three, not for 56 and not for both directions. If the transliteration's convention of numbering the radial lines from about half past nine is kept, twelve o'clock falls roughly six places on from the first radial line (two and a half hours of twelve, over 28 slots); I have not measured angles on the scan, so the three line ids must be fixed by someone who does, before any list is consulted. For the nominal length association already reported with a reversed alignment: it is described as a reverse alignment; if that means counter-clockwise, the script's direction does not support it and it would not be among the alignments to test. I did not check its starting slot against the gap. Limits: the heavy paint on one sector could be a painter's accident; the gaps could mark where each ring of text happened to close, not where the series begins; and eight sectors against twenty-eight bars has no obvious meaning in any mansion scheme I know, which a proposal for this page should address. Addendum, fixing the three line ids without measuring: the pinned transliteration gives a clock position on every radial line of this page (I had overlooked that; my earlier search for such markers covered label lines only). By those markers the radial line at twelve o'clock is f69v.9, with f69v.8 at half past eleven and f69v.10 at a quarter past twelve; the first radial line, f69v.4, is at half past nine, so twelve o'clock is five places on, not the 'roughly six' I estimated above. On the scan the short word standing over the bar at twelve o'clock is consistent with the transliteration's reading of f69v.9, as far as I can read it. The three alignments proposed are therefore: clockwise, starting at f69v.8, at f69v.9 and at f69v.10, and no others. One more candidate cue comes from the transliteration itself and should be weighed against the gap: its last radial line, f69v.31 at a quarter to nine, is the only radial line it gives as two words, and the transcriber chose to begin just after it; whether that reflects something on the page (a wider space, a different hand) or only convention I did not check, and if it is taken as a start cue it adds a fourth alignment at f69v.4, to be declared with the other three before any list is tried.
check: On the two scan regions named: confirm a blank gap in each of the three text rings at the top, wider than the word spaces beside it; count the rays of the central star; confirm that exactly one sector is painted solid and that it lies under the gaps. Then confirm from the transliteration's clock markers, and on the scan, that f69v.8, f69v.9 and f69v.10 are the radial words nearest twelve o'clock. The proposal fails if the gaps do not line up, or if a second sector is painted like the first.
